decision.rationale: PRR-019 is resolved and every existing local and exact-head CI gate passes, but PRR-020 proves that a post-dispatch unknown Accessibility action timeout is exposed to protocol consumers as retryable, contradicting the PR contract and permitting duplicate mutating actions.

findings.title: A dispatched action timeout is incorrectly advertised as retryable
findings.observation: The warm action path returns a worker timeout without internal fallback, but accessibility_action converts both pre-dispatch and post-dispatch timeouts to the same generic ComputerUseStatus.TIMEOUT. The protocol adapter marks every timeout retryable, so the top-level observation and nested ToolError expose retryable true even after the worker received the action.
findings.trigger: The action worker receives an AXPress request and begins the action, but no response arrives before the deadline; a run_command caller follows the protocol retryability classification.
findings.impact: A caller can retry an unknown mutating outcome and execute the same UI side effect twice. Suppressing the package's own one-shot fallback does not protect a consumer that relies on the public retryable field.

evidence.description: The worker timeout is converted to a generic Accessibility action timeout without preserving whether dispatch occurred.
The new warm action path returns the worker result directly and performs no one-shot fallback.
The protocol adapter marks every ComputerUseStatus.TIMEOUT retryable and copies that value into ToolError.
The PR merge-readiness public contract says action worker timeout or protocol failure is non-retryable after dispatch.

An exact-head synthetic worker recorded AXPress and withheld its response. The protocol result was timeout with failureKind accessibility_action_timeout and retryable true, with zero fallback calls; a retryable-false assertion exited 1.
The existing real-worker dispatched-timeout regression proves one dispatch and zero fallback calls but does not assert top-level or nested retryability.

findings.remediation: Preserve whether an action crossed the dispatch boundary and emit retryable false for post-dispatch timeout or unknown outcomes at both protocol levels. A pre-dispatch zero-write timeout may remain retryable only when reliably distinguished; conservatively making every Accessibility action timeout non-retryable is also safe. Align documentation with the implemented contract.
findings.verification: Extend the real dispatched-timeout regression to assert one recorded action, zero internal fallback calls, and top-level plus nested retryable false. Add a separate pre-dispatch timeout assertion for the chosen safe retry policy, then rerun package, root, framing and deadline, release, and exact-head CI gates.

findings.title: Expired queued actions were dispatched before timeout was reported
findings.observation: The former worker could exhaust its deadline waiting for the lock and still write. The current implementation serializes within the budget, bounds lock acquisition by remaining time, checks after acquisition, and checks again after startup and readiness before writing.
findings.trigger: Another request holds the worker lock beyond this request timeout, or startup reaches readiness but completion returns after the same deadline.
findings.impact: Before remediation, an action could begin after its caller timeout. Both repaired paths now return before dispatch and preserve a healthy worker.

evidence.description: One monotonic deadline now covers serialization, bounded lock acquisition, startup and readiness, the pre-write gate, and response waiting.
Real subprocess tests prove zero frames and same-process follow-up for lock contention and delayed startup completion.
The prior 0.1-second request completed while the lock remained held, wrote zero frames, returned timeout 124, and preserved the same process.

findings.remediation: Completed: bound lock waiting and startup by the request deadline, check again before writing, return pre-dispatch timeout with zero frames, and preserve a healthy worker.
findings.verification: Completed: both zero-write counterexamples, same-process follow-up, framing stress, warning-as-error package tests, repository tests, preflight, wheels, and exact-head CI passed.

required_actions.action: Distinguish post-dispatch unknown action outcomes from safe pre-dispatch expiration, emit retryable false after dispatch at both protocol levels, add protocol assertions, and synchronize the declared contract.
Prevent dispatch after queue or startup consumes the deadline, preserve a healthy worker, and add zero-write regressions.

limitations: This review is authoritative only for head 002fd7226634c7777e07416cb2e4401843e7b2b0.
The post-dispatch reproduction uses a synthetic worker and temporary marker and does not execute a real macOS Accessibility action.
The generic timeout-to-retryable mapping existed on the base branch, but this PR adds a default warm action path that reaches it and explicitly adds a contrary after-dispatch contract.
No fresh real desktop mutation, signed helper, or release publication was performed.
Private raw observations and unrelated dirty worktree files were excluded.
The GitHub PR remains draft and its platform body still describes the old 07fa052 request-changes snapshot.
assumptions: Protocol consumers may use retryable to decide whether an automatic or manual retry is safe; this is the field's backend recovery purpose.
A mutating request becomes an unknown outcome once write and flush cross the worker dispatch boundary, so response loss must not be advertised as safely retryable.
Pre-dispatch expiration may be retryable only when the implementation reliably preserves and propagates its zero-write state.
The current release record satisfies the MR-level changelog gate; an additional entry for each review-only remediation commit is not required.
